repl.title: Adaptive proposals for nonparametric equation-of-state inference with RIFT: iterative Gaussian-process refinement in a compressed sequence representation
repl.summary: Nonparametric equation-of-state (EOS) models have two practical problems for Bayesian inference: too many parameters, introducing observationally inaccessible degrees of freedom; and no painless route to adaptive refinement, necessary to forecast future observing scenarios. In this work we address both problems, providing a framework for adaptive nonparametric EOS sampling which simultaneously provides insight into the observationally-accessible effective dimensions. Applied to a published Gaussian-process ensemble, this analysis reveals substantial sound-speed freedom beyond what observations demand. Conversely, by concrete example, we demonstrate that often-used schemes to use many EOS realizations will invariably break down when challenged by new physics, as the observationally-accessible dimension increases substantially. These functional adaptive sampling tools provide a path forward to efficient computation, interpretation, and discovery for future analyses of cold, beta-equilibrium nuclear matter.

repl.title: Discovery of the Slowest Radio Pulsar in the Small Magellanic Cloud
repl.summary: We report the discovery of a new radio pulsar PSR J0103$-$72 in the Small Magellanic Cloud (SMC) through a reanalysis of Parkes/Murriyang archival observations targeting supernova remnants and pulsar-wind nebulae in the SMC. Previously two pulsars were discovered in these observations, and PSR J0103$-$72 is the third which we independently detected in two observations of its target field. It has a spin period of 1.327 sec and a dispersion measure (DM) of $272\pm13~\mathrm{pc\,cm^{-3}}$, making it the slowest known radio pulsar in the SMC with the second-highest DM. We did not identify any plausible supernova remnant or pulsar-wind nebula associated with the pulsar. Subtracting the predicted Galactic foreground leaves a DM contribution of $\sim 230$--$242~\mathrm{pc\,cm^{-3}}$, which may suggest a long path through the ionized medium of the SMC, enhanced ionized gas along the sightline, or both. Although these data had previously been searched using both FFT and fast folding algorithms, our FFT-based reprocessing found PSR J0103$-$72 through search techniques which have previously been highly effective in discovering a large number of pulsars in other surveys. This discovery shows that candidates with weak Fourier-domain significance can reveal faint, narrow-duty cycle pulsars missed in earlier extragalactic pulsar searches.

repl.title: History of Turn-Ons - the irregular 35-day clock - of Hercules X-1
repl.summary: Hercules X-1 and Centaurus X-3 are the first ever detected - and as such identified - binary X-ray pulsars. Here we concern ourselves with the 35-day flux modulation of Her X-1, immediately found at its discovery, together with the binary period of 1.7 days and the pulsation with 1.24 s. The 35-day flux modulation shows two flux maxima, the so-called Main-On and the Short-On (with reduced flux). As noticed early on, the period, or the length of the cycle, is variable. The system constitutes an irregular clock, with a more or less stable mean period of near 34.85 d. We consider the repeated rapid increases of the flux from the off-state to the Main-On (the socalled Turn-Ons) as the best timing marker to study this clock. Here we present a complete list of Turn-On times over 55 years, from the discovery of Her X-1 to today (2026), based on historic work from the literature and on observational data provided by five monitoring instruments. We identify to following basic features of the irregular 35-day clock: The Turn-Ons show preference to occur at orbital phases 0.25 and 0.75. The duration of the 35-day cycle clusters around three discrete values - 20.0, 20.5 and 21.0 orbital cycles with a dominant peak at 20.5 Porb (57%). The long-term trend in the 35-day period duration is seen in the O-C (Observed minus Calculated) diagram. There are two sections, separated by the long Anomalous Low of 1999/200 (AL3), which can be modeled by parabolic functions with a smooth evolution of the 35-day period. A medium-term variation is observed in the form of Anomalous Lows, an essential shut-off (at least of soft) X-rays. We find an apparent underlying period of 5.4 yr. There are short-term (hundreds of days) variations (in part quasi-periodic) overlaid to the long-term trend. Straight ups and downs in the O-C diagram, demonstrating rather rapid 35 day period changes.

repl.title: APOLLO-Timing: Annealed Phase - Orbit Lattice Linking across Observations for Binary Pulsar Timing
repl.summary: Sparse observations of binary pulsars can leave the orbit and the pulse count across observing gaps uncertain. We present APOLLO-Timing, a Bayesian phase-orbit lattice method that fits timing parameters together with integer pulse offsets between observing sessions. To validate candidate phase connections, we refit the timing model at fixed pulse numbers using the Python pulsar timing package PINT. We demonstrate the method on PSR J1912-1215, discovered in the CRAFTS survey. A preliminary Keplerian fit to variations in the apparent spin period and its derivative did not phase-connect 96 times of arrival (TOAs) spanning 1438.07 days in 23 sessions. Starting from its position, spin frequency $F_0$, and first time derivative $F_1$ estimated in that fit, with dispersion measure fixed, APOLLO-Timing recovers the orbit and a unique best-supported phase-connected solution without supplied orbital parameters. A repeat full-data blind search recovers the same pulse counts in 914.0 s, including the final fit. Setting the initial $F_1$ to zero in the 17-, 18-, and 19-session subsets also recovers the reference path. The solution gives $P_b=17.526$ days, $x=23.448$ light-seconds, $e=2.65\times10^{-5}$, $\chi^2=188.01$, and a weighted rms residual of $5.08\,\mu\mathrm{s}$. For a pulsar mass of $1.4\,M_\odot$ and inclination of $60^\circ$, the inferred companion mass is $0.67\,M_\odot$, favoring a CO/ONeMg white dwarf.

repl.title: Ultra-high-energy cosmic rays require metal-rich sources
repl.summary: The elemental composition of ultra-high-energy cosmic rays (UHECRs) must be evaluated at a given rigidity rather than energy to compare with candidate elemental abundances, such as those of low-energy cosmic rays seeding the acceleration of UHECRs. We determine the UHECR composition from fits to Pierre Auger Observatory data and evaluate the resulting abundances at fixed rigidity. We identify two classes of solutions consistent with measurements above $10^{17.8}$ eV: one in which the hydrogen flux at Earth is dominated by secondary nucleons produced by photodisintegration of heavier nuclei in extragalactic photon fields, and a second in which this contribution is less pronounced. Only the latter, which yields a mixture of primary and secondary protons at Earth, allows a hydrogen abundance at the source comparable to that of low-energy cosmic rays. However, both classes of solutions require an overabundance of nuclei in the silicon-iron group. Other source models from the literature also fail to reproduce the full elemental composition. The metallicity of UHECRs thus differs markedly from that of all candidate seed populations considered, leaving the origin of the heavy-element excess unresolved.

repl.title: NuSTAR view of the NGC 4151 corona: thermal balance and astroparticle constraints
repl.summary: I present a comprehensive analysis of all publicly available NuSTAR observations of the nearby Seyfert galaxy NGC 4151 (2012--2024). The hard X-ray continuum is well described by thermal Comptonization in a hot corona, with electron temperatures $kT_{\rm e} \approx 40-125$ keV and optical depths $\tau \approx 0.4-1.2$ (slab geometry). A clear anti-correlation between $kT_{\rm e}$ and $\tau$ is observed, consistent with a thermostat behavior with constant Compton parameter $\gamma \approx 3.12$ calculated according to Sunyaev and Titarchuk (1980). Variability on timescales of hours constrains the size of the emitting region to $R \approx 250-1200 r_{\rm g}$, corresponding to moderate compactness values $\ell \lesssim 4$. The source occupies the same region of the compactness--temperature plane as other local Seyferts, with no evidence for pair runaway. I then explore two astroparticle implications. The IceCube neutrino excess reported toward NGC 4151 corresponds to $L_\nu/L_X \approx 0.3\%$, an energetically negligible contribution that does not alter the observed coronal energy balance. An additional injection of pairs from the hypothetical X17 boson cannot produce significant changes, unless the injection rate exceeds the photoproduction one, but no anomalies were found in the present data set. The NuSTAR data thus provide no evidence for either a significant neutrino cooling channel or an X17-related pair injection in the corona of NGC 4151.

repl.title: Discovery of a likely supermassive neutron star in a remarkably wide binary
repl.summary: Supermassive neutron stars ($M \gtrsim 2\ M_{\odot}$) provide stringent constraints on the equation of state of dense matter. We report the discovery of a wide binary system composed of a red giant star and an invisible companion with an orbital period $P\approx 1218\pm3$ days and a comparatively low eccentricity $e\approx 0.09\pm0.01$ (with $1 \sigma$ uncertainty). By combining radial velocity measurements from the Large Sky Area Multi-Object Fiber Spectroscopic Telescope and the Apache Point Observatory Galactic Evolution Experiment (APOGEE) with astrometric data from {\it Gaia} DR2 and DR3 catalogues, we derive a Keplerian orbit with an inclination angle $i\approx73^{\circ}\pm11^{\circ}$. The unseen companion has a mass in the range of 1.8--2.8 $M_{\odot}$ (spanning the full spread of all estimates), with a best-fit value of $2.20^{+0.14}_{-0.13}$ $M_{\odot}$. This potentially places the unseen companion within the mass gap between neutron stars and black holes. Spectral disentangling using high-resolution near-infrared APOGEE spectra shows no absorption features from an additional component, suggesting the presence of a compact object: either a supermassive neutron star or a low-mass black hole. The wide, low-eccentricity orbit is difficult to explain through standard binary evolution channels, pointing to the need for improved theoretical models to account for such systems.

repl.title: The symplectic geometry of the black hole photon shell
repl.summary: The unstably bound, critical null geodesics of the Kerr spacetime form a distinguished class of orbits whose properties govern observables such as the photon ring and the high-frequency component of black-hole ringdown. This set of orbits defines a codimension-two submanifold of the null-geodesic phase space known as the photon shell. In this work we investigate the photon shell's intrinsic symplectic geometry. Using the induced symplectic form, we construct the canonical volume form on the shell and compute the differential phase-space volume it encloses as a function of radius -- equivalently, the radial density of states. In the near-extremal limit the photon shell bifurcates into near-horizon and far-region components; we find that approximately $3\%$ of the shell's phase-space volume resides in the near-horizon component. We also analyze a thickening of the photon shell that includes near-critical orbits, and compute its differential phase-space volume. Beyond their intrinsic theoretical interest, these results may inform the interpretation of high-resolution observations of spinning black holes.

repl.title: The Lumina Project: The Demographics of Active Galactic Nuclei from Quasars to Little Red Dots at $z\geq 3$
repl.summary: High-redshift active galactic nuclei (AGN) serve as powerful probes of early black-hole growth, galaxy formation, and the evolving intergalactic medium (IGM). In this work, we use Lumina, a cosmological radiation-hydrodynamic simulation spanning the epochs of hydrogen and helium reionization, which combines a large $(500\,{\rm cMpc})^3$ volume with $2\times 6000^3$ resolution elements, to explore high-redshift AGN. The simulation self-consistently follows hundreds of millions of galaxies and supermassive black holes (SMBHs), together with their impact on the ionization and thermal state of the IGM. We exploit this uniquely large dynamic range to predict multi-band AGN luminosity functions (LFs) at $z \geq 3$, from hard X-rays to the mid-infrared. These predictions encompass both moderately luminous quasars and the faint ``Little Red Dots'' (LRDs) uncovered by JWST. We develop an empirical model that maps simulated SMBHs onto observed AGN using bolometric and extinction/absorption corrections for canonical AGN and LRDs, and in which SMBHs with $M_{\rm BH}\leq 10\,M_{\rm seed} \sim 10^{7}\,{\rm M}_{\odot}$ stay in the LRD phase with a duty cycle of $30\%$. This simple framework reproduces the observed LFs and clustering of LRDs. Meanwhile, the pre-JWST quasar LF constraints are recovered, although we find that a $\sim 0.3$ dex log-normal scatter in bolometric luminosity is required to reproduce the bright end. We place the simulated AGN population in the cosmological context by quantifying the redshift evolution of AGN and LRD number densities, and their contributions to the integrated BH mass densities. The same AGN population is the dominant driver for the HeII reionization modelled self-consistently in Lumina. This empirical AGN model paves the way for general population-synthesis models of high-redshift AGN, including LRDs, in a unified cosmological framework.

repl.title: Short Gravitational-Wave Transients as Probes of Cosmic Domain Walls
repl.summary: GW190521 and GW231123 have been reported as short-duration gravitational-wave transients consistent with very massive binary black hole (BBH) coalescences whose inferred parameters, i.e., exceptionally high total masses and spin magnitudes, challenge standard isolated binary stellar evolution. We test a topological dark matter (TDM) interpretation invoking cosmic domain walls by fitting a physically motivated domain wall template to the LIGO Hanford and Livingston strain data. The BBH hypothesis is individually favored, with $\log_{10}\mathcal{B}_{\rm BBH/TDM}=12.2$ and $11.3$ for GW231123 and GW190521, respectively. However, these values are lower than those typically recovered from matched maximum a posteriori BBH waveforms injected into nearby noise segments. We further perform, for the first time, a joint fit in which domain wall signals from a single underlying scalar field are constrained simultaneously by both events. Although not favored over BBH signals, we find the two events are consistent with a common scalar field, with shared TDM parameters agreeing across independent noise realizations and sky locations. We further find that injected TDM transients are systematically recovered under the BBH hypothesis with large spin parameters, revealing a morphological degeneracy that could mask genuine domain wall signals. This analysis demonstrates that multi-event parameter consistency tests provide a new discriminant for domain wall dark matter searches in upcoming observing runs.

repl.title: The Fifth RIT Catalog of Binary Black Hole Simulations: Multiple-Resolution Studies of Eccentric Orbits
repl.summary: This fifth release of the RIT public catalog of numerical relativity binary black hole waveforms this http URL introduces an additional 248 configurations, prioritizing 197 newly simulated eccentric orbits. This update brings the catalog to a total of 2129 cases. All waveforms are corrected for center-of-mass drift and extrapolated to future null infinity. To rigorously estimate waveform errors, we conduct multiple-resolution convergence studies on 10 eccentric simulations (up to 33 orbits to merger) using three global resolutions increasing by factors of 1.2, plus a comprehensive six-resolution study for a single 18-orbit configuration. We evaluate waveform accuracy by computing mismatches against theoretical infinite-resolution extrapolations. Additionally, we analyze the convergence properties of key physical observables: merger times, number of orbits, final masses, final spins, recoil velocities, and the peak amplitude, frequency, and luminosity of the gravitational radiation.

repl.title: Gas-induced gravitational-wave dephasing and accretion periodicities of live post-Newtonian massive black hole binaries: warm disk
repl.summary: We perform 3D hydrodynamical simulations of an equal-mass quasi-circular live $10^6 {\rm M}_\odot$ massive black hole binary (MBHB) embedded in a prograde, locally isothermal circumbinary disk (CBD) with 0.1 aspect ratio. The binary evolves under the effect of gaseous torques and 2.5 post-Newtonian dynamics. We follow the gravitational-wave (GW) driven inspiral from 53 Schwarzschild radii ($r_s$) down to merger, over 1.5 years. Comparing the GW inspiral rate with the viscous inflow, we find the binary to decouple from the CBD just $\approx 2$ days before merger. We measure gas torques (gravitational and accretion) with and without concurrent GW emission, finding that their sums agree to within $\lesssim 5\%$ down to $25 r_s$. We then measure a gas-induced GW phase shift that peaks at $\approx 5\times10^{-4}$ rad near $45 r_s$, as the gas torque slows the inspiral, and then changes sign as the accreted mass accelerates it. It is LISA-detectable only at $z\lesssim 0.1$. We further characterize the mass accretion rate modulations. All three fundamental periodicities, associated with the "lump" at the inner cavity edge, the binary orbital period, and half of it, are shifted to lower frequencies by precession. We measure the shift at the orbital period, due to relativistic apsidal precession, in an inspiraling binary for the first time, and newly identify the other two as due to the precession of the eccentric cavity. Our results have implications for multi-messenger astronomy, since observation of accretion rate modulation by LSST/Roman surveys and phase-shift by LISA will provide crucial information on the complex environment surrounding MBHBs.

repl.title: Effect of post-recombination accretion on primordial binary black hole mergers within virialized dark matter halos
repl.summary: Gravitational waves from binary black hole mergers remain among primary sources for ground-based and space laser interferometers. Primordial binary black holes (PBHs) can form binaries in the early Universe or at the matter-dominated stage in virialized dark matter halos at redshifts $z\sim 7-15$. We study enhancement of primordial binary PBH merger rate in virialized dark matter halos due to baryon accretion in the post-recombination epoch within two accretion models onto individual PBH -- Bondi-Hoyle-Littleton (BHL) and Park-Ricotti (PR), representing two extreme cases of the accretion efficiency. We calculate modification of the initial PBH mass function and their fractional contribution to dark matter. A significant enhancement in the binary PBH merger rate is found for the late three-body channel, which was previously treated as subdominant. In the case of delayed virialization onset at $z<10$, merger rates of dynamically formed PBH binaries are limited by the existing LVK binary BH detections. An increased merger frequency is revealed for PBH binaries with highly asymmetric mass ratios. We also calculate expected detection rates of binary PBH mergers for the TianQin space-based gravitational-wave interferometer and show them to be optimistic in the BHL accretion case even for very low initial PBH abundances $f_\text{PBH}\sim 10^{-6}$.

repl.title: Analytic parity-violating greybody factors of a dynamical Chern-Simons black hole
repl.summary: We study the low-frequency scattering of gravitational and pseudoscalar waves off a non-rotating black hole in dynamical Chern-Simons (dCS) gravity, where the axial (odd-parity) gravitational sector is irreducibly coupled to the dynamical pseudoscalar while the polar sector remains general relativistic. Working to first order in the dimensionless coupling zeta = (l_CS/M)^4 and using matched asymptotic expansions, we obtain, for the quadrupole (l=2) channel, an exact closed form for the graviton-to-pseudoscalar conversion probability and a high-precision analytic reconstruction of the absorption (greybody) asymmetry. Both reduce to combinations of pi^4, pi^2, and rational numbers, with no ln2 or odd-zeta terms in the reconstructed basis; the transmission-phase sector, by contrast, is governed by an analytically derived static integral involving Apery's constant zeta(3), with its matching prefactor identified numerically. The parity-violating reflection-phase asymmetry is strongly suppressed at low frequency -- well below the parity-even general-relativistic reflection phase -- so that any polarization rotation imprinted on the reflected wave is negligible, while a subleading O(omega*zeta) asymmetry remains in the transmitted phase. These effects are intrinsically strong-field and low-frequency: the normalized flux asymmetries are consistent with a 1/(M*omega)^2 falloff in the geometric-optics limit, where the leading remaining flux effect is conversion loss. The matched-asymptotic results are checked against direct two-channel integration, and the integral determining the absorption asymmetry is evaluated to high precision within an analytically controlled transcendental basis. The coefficients provide analytic targets linking dCS parity violation in absorption and mode conversion to the axial/polar quasinormal-mode splitting.
